blocks.x: You say he was here on a show? He wrestled Big Chief Moore?
You knew him, eh?
Yeah, a little bit. I doubt if he knows me. He was here and you gave him a job or something, huh?

Yeah, I was the first man to hire him. Hire him from the Lyrics Theater. He was taking him up to Vashville. That's the first job he played. He was taking off his shoes, man, to play. That guy played some trombone though that night.
Did Moore come from Oklahoma or someplace up there? Do you know? Who? This Indian trombone player.
I don't know where he's from.
He's a FEMA Indian. He's from New Mexico or Arizona.
He's from overseas somewhere.
No, he's from New Mexico or Arizona, not too far. Yeah.
Boy where he could play. Mm-hmm.
What did he do with his shoes off? Did he play the trombone with his feet or something?
No, he'd take the shoes off, rest his feet.
Oh. I thought maybe he was one of those trick trombones. You've seen those guys.
No, he wanted to take his shoes off. And he said, you're going to hear some trombone playing now, boy. Take my shoes off. And he pulled them shoes off and rest them dogs. I mean he played too.
Who else did he play with around town? Well he played the Celestan.
I thought that's who he played.
He told me about it once.

And after they left Celestan band, they had made a couple of tools all up and down the country. And they went down to Florida. A boy from over the lake seen him in the tool. Tool B, that's where Punch was down there. He says he seen him down in Florida. I said, I wish I would get hold of him.
And I never did see that man no more.

And he came in. I was talking to John Porter and John Porter told me he was in town a few weeks ago. Some place they played up here somewhere. And John Porter, he went home and passed away. He just had told me, he said his heart was bad anyway. Because we was kidding. He said, now there's Jim, he's making his money. And he's not playing. See, when they played the student watches, Jim had to cut out. He wasn't knowing that.
That was a tuxedo band. Yeah.
That boy got the music brought there. Well, seems like he didn't understand. He couldn't cut it.
I wonder if we could start out by asking your name, you know, just state your name and your age when you were born. And we'll have that on the tape then.
You want it now?
Yeah. Start right now.

My name is Isaiah Morgan. Born 1897. Seventh day of April. And where were you born? In Bytranville, Louisiana. That's down the country. That's twenty-eight miles down the Mississippi River. On this side? Yeah.
Well, where's your family from? Huh?

Where's your family from? Is your father and mother from down there? Oh, everybody's from down there. Everybody's from down there. Everybody's from down there. Everybody's from down there. Yeah. I mean, I'm sorry. I'm sorry.
I'm sorry.
I'm sorry. I'm sorry.
I'm sorry. I'm sorry.
I'm sorry.
I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.
Everybody's from down there. Everybody. The whole bunch.
Did your father play music at all?
No. He was a great church member. Oh. Did he? Mother was a church member. Uh-huh. Just the boys started out music.
Did your father sing in church or something? What church was it, by the way?
Well, it was a Baptist church. A little country church.
How much older was Sam than you?

Well, no, I couldn't tell. It was about, really, I don't know, because this boy here died. The other brother died here a couple of years back. It was, uh, he was 66 years old. And Sam must have was going in 66 when he died. See?
When did Sam die? About what year?

On a carnival day. Mm. We was playing music uptown when he did, we got the news that he was dead. Cool. Right there on St. Louis street, St. Louis and Begundray. That's where we were living at. He died with a overnight pneumonia. See, he had had a stroke, you see? And then he had got better and he was playing music and just set out on the banquet late at night, like some fellas you know, with some of the boys, and he caught an overnight pneumonia in the cold, you see? That's where he died. I've never heard of such a thing.
That's fantastic. Yeah. Now, how many brothers are there in all?

Well, all I know is it was six of us living. It was four dead. I don't know anything about them, see? It was before my time. We had the youngest brother. He was 40. That was the youngest brother. He was 42 years old, I think. That was one next to Albert. Then Al. Then next is Andrew. And next is me. And the next was Robert. And the next was Sam, you see?
Well, what about the youngest? Did he play music at all? No, no.

Him and Robert didn't play no music. We tried to get him to play piano, but he didn't like that. He didn't, he just liked to write these numbers at this time, you see? When these, these lots was going on. Well, that's what he liked.
Oh, he was a writer.
Yeah.
Well, how did you get started in music yourself? Did you pick it up yourself?

I just picked it up my own self. I used to listen at these records. Wind King. I used to hear Wind King. Wind King, I think that's his name. And I wanted to learn music. So I picked that up my own self. I always wanted to blow my brothers home, but he didn't want me to blow it, you see? And blow on it, and after I found I could feel it, well, I just went on. Well, Jim Lill was the first man, stopped me out. We went down to Beuris, Louisiana, playing a carnival dance down there. Well, I couldn't play nothing. He was playing violin, you see? And we went down there, well, he just carried me along. Jim, all the Jim's was down there. And we played down there, well, he just made out. And when I come back and throw the next, it was Halloween knife after carnival, yeah. I think it was Easter Sunday. We played on Barrick Street. I had a four piece job. Well, I could play about four, four songs. And I'd take the chance and went down and play that and made that change. Then Easter Sunday, Easter Saturday, we went back down the country where I could play better, you see? And from that on, I just went on. Well, then I got organized me a band, Young Morgan band. And after we had that band, and we was doing so good, I had a headquarters on the domain between Liberty and St. Claude at Jim Crow House. Jim Robinson would call him. And after we had put a sign up there, Young Morgan Band, for all occasions. So after we started playing, everybody started to hire us, Young Sam Morgan. Well, we come to find we was stronger just in my other brother, you see? So that's the way we started playing. Then again, I started taking lessons from old man, old man Delmar, a man from Baton Rouge. I had him come there to teach me and Jim Robinson. Well, I seen where Jim wasn't making no headway and I just went on by myself. So I taken about 12 lessons and he showed me and I understand what he showed me. He showed me the line and the four spaces and after I found that out, I could, the next night he come, I could tell him what he showed me last night, pass. Then he said, well, we're going to take you on a little song. And he take me a little song in the method and I could play that. And after that, I started rearranging music, my own stuff. I go to the world line and get the manuscript, piano copy and get the manuscript and I'd copy my numbers and get the choruses. And anything I could hear, anything, anything I could hear, any of them bands play on the record, I could play. I didn't miss it because I played straight just like they played it, you know, with none of this progressive jazz or nothing like that. I always liked to play my music where people could understand it.
I was wondering, what were those first four tunes that you played? Do you remember the first four tunes that you played?
The first four? Margie. That was the first thing. That was the first thing. That was the first of us. And Dolomite, Dolomite, Dolomite, Dolomite of Dynamite. Now the others, I don't know.
About what year was it you got those numbers?
Well, I got this, no, got me hooked then.
Yeah, I just wondered about how old you were. Were you 15 or 20?
No, I was, I had been to the dorm and come back, I was round 20, round about 20, 21, 22 years old, something like that.
Did you have a cornet when you started or a trumpet?
I wore a cornet. I wore a cornet. I wore two cornet.
What kind of a horn did you like to make?

I just, any, any, any, any, uh, world I had with CG corn was to go then. Then the next, I had a, a king trumpet I got from Mobile. Then the next, I got a, a king trumpet. I had two king trumpets. And I had some other kind of trumpet. I forgot this kind of trumpet that I had. Well, anyway, I was, I used those three and wore them out. I just figured they wasn't suit me so I just got back on, on the CG corn, got me a CG corn. I got it over the lake then now.
You play trumpet now or a cornet?

I have, uh, old, old trumpet. And I still, you know, if I start to play it I'm gonna buy a brand new one. I'm gonna get me a, a Martin. And that'll be the last one. Because they don't make these trumpets gold no more. They make them lack it, you see. Yeah. And they, they don't last. They, they, they smell so bad, you see. Keep, gotta keep them clean all the time. And if you, you shine them too much, you, where's all that lack at all?
What kind of a hard did Sam play? I guess he started on cornet too, of course, wasn't he?

He, he started on cornet. He started on CG corn. Then my brother sent him, after he had fell sick, and he got better enough to play, he sent him another, sent him a trumpet from New York, a huge CG corn. That was CG corn.
Did he play trumpet too or did he stick to the cornet all the time?

No, he played trumpet. He played trumpet at the last, on the last session you see. At first he used to use cornet, you see. They said cornet was louder in the trumpets, but the trumpet was further, the sound would go further you know.
Did you notice much difference in the tone when you played the change from one to the other?

Well I, I did. And I still know. The trumpets, the trumpets, with the use now, and at that time you have, you have a further range of blowing, you know. Yeah. The cornet, they're louder. They're much louder, they're close you see, in the close place.

Can you tell us something more about your brother, since he isn't here anymore to talk for himself, about his first band? Do you remember who was in his first band and the band that made the records and all through that? Anything you can remember about him for a while?

Well, he didn't make no records until he got with me. The first band he had, it was Joe Watson, clarinet player, T-Boy, that was the bass player, that was the one my brother was trying to think of, a little short fellow. Then, the guitar player was Butler Red, we call him Guy A. I think I see, well, the drummer was Alfred William.
Trombone?

Trombone was, uh, Yankee. And his, uh, they only had six pieces. But they didn't make no recording until I take him with us. See, they was trying to, seems like they were trying to double cross him after he got sick, figured he couldn't play anymore. And trying to put Willie Pajot in his place when they went to Mobile. They went down there and they made a failure. So, the man came and told him, says, uh, that wasn't Sam Morgan Band. What do you heard? So, I told him, I said, we'll take you with us. Oh, he didn't want that. But the only time he did any traveling went away anyway further when he got with us. When he found out we were strong enough, we had two trumpets then. We had two trumpets. We had oil on saxophone. We had Andrew on sax and clarinet. We had Jim Robinson on trombone. And had Jim on bass. We had Johnny Devin on banjo. And we had Lil Roy Even. He's dead. We had him on drums. Well, we always did pick up a piano player, automobile. We didn't carry no piano player, you see. So, we had a strong band. Well, we went to Chicago. We played down there for Kid Eury. We stayed in Chicago. I think we carried an excursion from there. Stayed down there for about three days. And we played down to Indiana. Gary, Indiana. And from that on, I just went on to Sam Morgan's band. And everywhere we went, it was Sam Morgan. Well, we started going to Mobile. We used to draw from 33 to 3400 head of people every Monday night. Well, we played on it at Brooklyn Park. And they had this Pensacola band. My brother Al was playing with them. We had this Hall playing with their band. Pensacola. That's all you could hear was Pensacola band. Well, after we come through there, well, you couldn't hear nothing no more about them. We had to give my brother fair to come home.
Which hall was this that was with them? The Blar and Ed Blar Hall?
Yeah, that same hall in New York. Oh, Edmont.
Yeah. Yeah.
There was me in Pensacola, raising up a breeze.
Mack Thomas, would that be the ones?
You mean Mack the trumpet player?
Yeah. Was he the trumpet player with that band?
No, he had his own band.
Was it Lee Collins went over that one time?
I don't know. I think Lee was playing with them, if I'm mistaken. I don't know who was the trumpet player, but I know Mack wasn't playing with them.
When did you let Sam in your band? About what, yeah, do you remember?
Well, it was after, after he got well about. No, I think it was 36, he died in 36. He was playing then. It must, it might have been about 32 or 33.
But when did you make the records about what you have? Yeah.
Now that's something I never kept, kept no record of that. Yeah. We, we, we played for the Columbia Broadcasting people. They came down here and we record for them.
You never heard the building?
Where, where did you make the records? Well, we made them at the wire lines upstairs in the back, in that, of course, it wasn't none of these things. Electric or anything.
Well it is. It was electric in those days.

Man, they had, these things you had to get there and blow and didn't use no drum, wouldn't leave no drums. They didn't take no drum. Did the drummer play with you and put them in back? Yeah, he played, but he had to play cymbal, not no drum. We blowed in, it's a big, each one of it was at these things, look like these things you sing through a microphone. A big horn like that.
Yeah.
That's what we had to make them records part. It wasn't made like these fellas make, they could pick up nothing.
And who was your drummer on the record?
Roy, Roy Abison. That was a nice little drummer.
But who took his place after he died?
Well, after he died, well we didn't have nobody else.
Look at that. Well this is a surprise. I let my dog walk in. You know, I looked at that thought hard. There's another tourist gonna buy a record, you know, and then I recognized him.
Yeah, I recognized him right away. I didn't even recognize him.
It's been many years since you've seen him, since he's seen you too.
I wanted to see him anyway when he was down here before, but I didn't see him. I seen his brother. Oh, that was Mac. Mac was playing with them.
Yeah, Mac. You want a cigarette? No.
I just smoked him in. Edmund Hall. Isn't him Edmund Hall? Yeah.
Mm-hmm.

Yeah, these guys, I didn't have a chance to tell them about that Pensacola band. We threw that band apart when we got started to go into Mobile. Yeah. I see. We were talking about those records you made.
Is there anything else? Oh, I was gonna ask about how come you made those spirituals, you know? Did they play those spirituals in the dance hall, like Sing On, Glory Land? Well, no. No, we didn't.

We played those, just like those Maypoles in Mobile on parades, you see? But we didn't play no spirituals, hymns in no dance hall, like these fellas do in here. Uh-huh. I think we played, uh, we made, uh, Sing On, Over in the Glory Land. And what else? We, uh, three spirituals, but we didn't play them in, uh...
Did any other bands ever play them in those days in the dance halls, like they do now? Uh-huh. The Saints go marching in, they play all the time.

Uh-huh. Well, they, they, taking that for real ragged. Well, they do's that, but we never did play nothing like that. They'd copy that from Louis playing it on the record, and they just start to playing it on the dance, in the dance hall, because people would ask them. You see, any place I would play that, ask me for that, I'd tell them I wouldn't play that. So, I never did play it. So, uh, I don't know. Maybe some of them, a lot of them be playing them songs we played. Those hymns. Only thing we played are what we record. Bug loose and struck. And everybody talking about Sammy. Sammy got the best score of the year. I can't even think of how them things go. Nothing.
Oh, who took Roy Evans' place? You say you didn't have a drummer for a while. Who? After Roy Evans died. He left your band, Roy Evans, the drummer?
No, he died here.
Mm-hmm.

Well, I think we're taking Alfred Williams, Sam's old drummer. He's still living here. He's here now. Yes, I know. Well, he played with me. He used to make all the trips with me. We didn't have no drummer. Well, Sean was the first drummer that we had. Then after Sean left, we'd taken Roy. Sean used to get drunk and then claim he was losing his mind. And we'd taken this boy. And he married a girl over in Mississippi. And that told him to stay with the band. And he died. And we'd taken Alfred. And just anybody would come along with some time. Let's see. We used Lionel Tarraganda a while. Let's see for some of the trips. Like we'd go to Bugger Lucy. When we could get him. When this old lady would leave and go. Well, it was a hard thing for us to have a drum player, regular. But after Alfred, he came from Texas, we started using him. And from there, the band began just breaking up. After Roy left, that was all.
Oh, who did you use on piano on the records?
We didn't use no piano.
No piano, did we? No piano.

I used to use a girl called May. I don't know if that woman is dead. She's first sight reader, you know. Used to play at this club on Rampo Street. What's the name of that club? On Rampo Street. That young men's business club. Well, always had all those engagements to play there. Lots of time would be in the evening. Well, I'd get May to come in to help us out. Because when you come there, they bring you music right there, and they know Raheisa. See? And she was the kind of woman to help you out, you see?
That's the place in about the 200 block of North Rampo Street?
Yes, between Aberville and Bienville. Oh, yeah. Yeah, that's where the athletic club is. That's the place. That's the place.

Well, to get back once more, we won't bother about the records anymore. Do you remember though, what they paid? Did they pay so much aside, or so much to date? They didn't have a union, I don't think much in those days, any regular scale for making records. About what did they pay? I'm not trying to put into your business.
Well, that's alright. They paid us $15 a side for the record, a piece. And the royalty, well, the man who had the songs- The composers of the royalty. Yeah, well, he got it.
Did you ever make any other records afterwards? Uh-uh.

Well, I had a chance to make records, but look what I was doing. But look where I had to go to make them. That was in- They want me to go to Johnson, Tennessee. And I didn't want to go up there, you see. Because you can't pick them on no fellas around there. The fellas are hard, man. To get them to go anywhere, to round them, but they're around here with the not complicated, watching old ladies or something. They ain't scared to leave home. Yeah. But what I'm thinking about, man, if I just could have got the recording bunch- Now these boys over the lake is working. That's the band that I want to put on the record. They can play anything. Little youngsters. See? Get the player, bass player, saxophone player, old saxophone player, used to be around here. He's Warren. He played just like oil. And he can play that new style, and old style, all that. And as far as you can think, he's right there with you. What's his name?
Oh, no, Warren.
Warren? Warren? Warren Bennett.
Warren Bennett.
He was from here, huh? No, he's from Bay St. Louis.
Oh, I didn't know him around here.
He been playing over here a while with this boy here. What's his name? He lived on Sinan Street. Played Sousa for him. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Gasseney Station. You get to a player, he works at that Navy's hospital down there.
That's over in Biloxi, all of these.

In Biloxi. And bass player, he's in Bay St. Louis. It don't take long to get them together because I have all them phone them, you know what I mean? Anytime I have a gig, I just ring them up and they'll come over and play. All of them got calls. Now for recording, them the only band that I see I would want to record some records.
Do they play the old style then?
Same as the bands do here. They can play the old style and play the youth style.
I was wondering about, maybe you told when I was running the machine and didn't hear, when you moved up from the country, how old were you? When did you move to New Orleans?
I moved the day after that 1915 storm. I don't blame you.
Had Sam in the other state or was Sam up here playing already?
Well, no Sam was up here.
He was up here.

Yeah. Then I had been coming up here. I had an auntie waking up on St. Charles Street, right St. Charles and Louisiana Avenue for a man from down the country down there. Well, I stayed up there with her a while before the storm. You know what I mean? I'd come and go, come and go. But I was in the country when that storm came up. And I was laying down in the bed and that 1915 storm came up. And when I seen that house on joint like that, I said, it's time for me to go. Fell apart up the rafters, huh? Yes. I mean, come on party. So I moved up. Went over to somebody else's house. And the Mississippi River man was boiling. Like he was angry.
That was down, way down below Violet. Is it farther than Pointe?
Oh man, that's 30 miles down. 30 miles away. That's the place at the place called Belay. Belay. Same as these Fools called. Old man John Diamond's place.
Was there any music much down in the country? Any of the bands or singers or what they had?

No. They had, they had Sam and them, they had a band once down there. They started the band and all musicians. And well I guess they think they was good anyhow. Well yeah, we had a man coming in, a trombone player coming down there teaching them. They was mixed from, from, from Ballad to Sin Sof. What was the brass band, you know? Oh yeah. Oh I can't think of this man's name. He used to come down there, he had a little train running down, Louisiana Southern, running down there. He used to come down there on the train and I think once a week teaching.
He was like Jim Humphries. Huh? He was like Jim Humphries, like Willie and Percy Humphries' grandfather. He was a teacher like that man. You know the following I'm talking about?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. His name was, I can't think of this man's name. Boy he was well known. Yeah.
Trombone, was it Perkins, what's his name, you know, the real light fella? Dave Perkins. Dave Perkins. Would it be him?
No, Dave Perkins used to work at Royal Iron. I didn't know that.
I'm sure.
Dave Perkins, with, Dave Perkins used to work at Royal Iron and everything. He had a whole lot of instruments and things.
Yeah, he could play a lot of many talents. He was a trombone player most of them.
Well, I wondered about that brass band. Did they play for parades? Did they have many parades down there in the country?
No, they didn't play many parades.
One second. I got my keys. I got my on a bell.
Is that the German or Willie Parker?
Yeah, I see him anytime. He lived right one block for me.
Yeah, how you doin'? We were happy to come out here for having an interview. Alright.
We didn't get settled when I had it. I, uh...
Was he in that band, Willie Parker by any chance?

No, he wasn't. No, he wasn't. He was gone by then. He was up here. He was one of these cats always, uh, play. I think we was playing with the Eureka, playing snare drum. No, he wasn't in those bands down there.
Was Sonny Henry down there then?
Well, Sonny was on the other side of the river. Oh, I see.
They had different bands on the other side. Yeah, yeah.
If they had a band over there, I don't know if they had a band over there. What do you got about that?
Oh, I don't know. Bill buys everything.
It's a hobby, you know.
Who are some of the other guys from down the river that you heard?
Well, uh, the fellas' trombone player, he died. John Williams, Beam, the trumpet player. He's dead. And all them fellas has died on out, man.

What about the Quackos? Did they come down there? You know Philip Pills? Cripple Pills? No, I don't know that. You didn't know Cripple Pills, the clarinet player? He's from Violet. Nanny, his brother, Nanny Quacko, played trumpet. Well, I didn't know he had a brother. But, uh, Phil, that's the name? That Cripple fellow? Yeah. Yeah, he's from, uh, he's from Violet, Louisiana. That's right down the road then.
That's 11 miles out of town. I just wondered if they came around Bertrand, Virginia, and they came around the river. No, no. No, no.
Well what kind of music did the brass band play? Did they play regular standard marches? Yeah. Hems or what?

They played marches, jazz numbers, I guess what they called you know at that time. They didn't understand, I don't guess they didn't understand much what they was doing anyway. But they wasn't up to like the fellas playing around here now, you know what I mean? Playing parades on the street. They had a band somewhere down on the other side of the river, I don't know who they was, from St. Sophie. They had a good band. They called him, you got a boy awake, they in the veteran hospital, call him Beam. Well he was really my cousin and he's Kent Sam. Sam was playing trumpet and he played trumpet. Well he had his band down there and Sam had his band up there around the ballet. But they, oh this fella was trying to figure, Frankie Doocy, that's the trombone player, was teaching them. Oh Doocy, Frankie?
Frankie Doocy.
That's the fella was teaching them. Wow.
That's a surprise. Was he much of a reader and all that, do you know? Doocy? Did he make any record?

Was he a reader? He was a good reader or what, do you know? Well I don't know, he was teaching them. Yeah, that's a surprise. And I never, I thought of him as a, mostly an ear man, I didn't know he was teaching them.
Well anyway, he was teaching them. And I don't tell you the facts, I don't know if any of them was reading at that time.

And because my brother Sam, he read when he was up here, I don't know what he did in the country, see. Me and Sam used to put them old hard numbers on us up there on the Estory Garden, I heard Al speaking about the Estory. He bring them numbers right there and let that place get full of people and then he'd draw them out there. Put them up there. But you hadn't rehearsed even? No, he said, who fall down, stay down. See I can't get you all to rehearse. Miss Trombone, Sally Trombone, all that's for trombone work. Well you see they didn't have Jim Hook because Jim had done played them numbers with Chris Kelly. You see? And he's a good year man already, and he's slick. And he had everything his way. And he said, now he'd bring them numbers, now I think he can catch me. But see I was playing first trumpet, you see? And the trombone part, all Jim wanted to do, the other corner leading, and he could harmonize some kind of way, and he hardly would go wrong. You see? Well that's the thing that saved him. Now I don't know why they, now Howard is another one. He's been playing a whole lot of stuff for Jim. And he didn't, don't worry Jim. I think that's why they turned that other boy off. Alvin, Alvin was a better musician in Howard, and he got better lips in Howard.

And I don't see why they turned that way. And I don't see why they turned anymore. I think he couldn't travel or something. Maybe I think he had a job here and they went on the road. Alvin didn't want to go on the road or something.

Because Jim, Jim is, and Howard is friends. And then they had them fired Howard. And I don't know why they had taken him back. And I could never get in touch with George and Lewis. I could never get that boy's phone number. I asked Jim his phone number. He told me, look in the phone book.
It's in the phone book.
But there's so many of them. It's the one on DeArmond Street.
Yeah, I'd look everywhere.
I have the number. I can give it to you after a while.
You'll get it.
There's several Joey's, Lewis's, but...

I tried to get him to play with me over the lake once or twice. When his wife, he married one of my cousins, the first wife, would die. Janette. Yeah. And I couldn't get him to come over the lake. Just for one night and get him. I tried to get this old boy Cleo. You know Cleo, the bass player? I heard about him, but he died before I got here. Boy, that was the coming bass player. He could play. He was playing with me. Then, uh... After he... Fooled on you and let's sit in the desk. I don't have no time for that kid. Fooled that boy. Made him stay here. Wouldn't let him come over the lake. I wanted to come over there in 41. On a regular job. Five years and five months. And he wouldn't let the boy... fool that boy. Stay here with him. Fooled on that old big band. He wasn't playing but a couple of nights. Week. Maybe about once. Twice a week. Then after he got disgusted he couldn't make no money, he gets out there and grabs a ship. Now he gonna go on the ship. Marine. And went out there. Time he got out there and them Japanese sunk it. He lost his soul.
Oh, do you remember when George Gaynor joined the band? He played with you, didn't he?
Well, he did after Johnny... after Johnny did.
Was he with you long? How long did he...

Oh yeah, he stayed with us a long time. George Gaynor stayed until we just broke up almost. He just said so wild and crazy. He can play pretty good banjo. I don't like the ghetto playing. He hits that old banjo so hard. Johnny had to build their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear What's the matter though? Everybody howl for the same long man, said, y'all better play. And every time we'd get on the stairs, that guy would go downstairs and we didn't know what it was all about. He cut that mic off, you see? So I seen him, I went downstairs, got out the stairs, went downstairs to see him doing something. And I come back and told the captain, I said, is nobody hearing nothing what we're playing coming up here? And the fella said, no, they got y'all cut off downstairs. So that started to mess up there with old fate, made him turn that mic on. Didn't want us to be here, you know what I mean? Of course the French market bunch was our bunch. You see, they was on the boat, riding on the boat that Sunday. They was going for Sam Morgan band. They wasn't worrying about the Fiat and Marble. He had, and that son had 10, 10 pieces, 12 pieces. And Dewey Jackson. And the man told him, says, I want to, before you all get down to that, the landing, say, I want to see what y'all going to do. And then people howling for Sam Morgan band. He said, well, we going to, say, just, we going to fix them. I said, yeah? All right, I'm going to hear. And he had one of these time clocks. Something that's set on there, times, time the music. He said, this band is hitting like a clock. And he says, he's going to play something. And they played a number. And I ain't forgot that number yet. And we didn't have that number. Well, that was all right. They didn't go for that. And we'd double around with some other old crazy song and toured feet to death. Well, anyway, we got that number. We got the name of that number and sent off and got it. And the father and son, we come back on that boat, and we played it for feet.
Was there a guy killed on that same boat? Which boat was that? Huh? Which boat was this, anyway, that you played on? The steamer capitol. And was that a guy killed on the capitol?
No.

Ain't nobody got killed on it. Not as I know. Well, I was going to ask about your band. I know it was very popular. Like you said, they're always yelling for Sam Morgan's band and so on. Was there anything that made your band different or better than the others? What was it? The beat? Did you have a better beat? Did you play better for the dancers? Or what do you think it was?

Well we played the same way because Sam, he's a man strictly for time. He didn't allow you to rush no time, you know what I mean? He had that swing. He had on our plyo court, Sam Morgan band with the swing. That's everywhere we go. Well, yeah, yeah, yeah, that's how it was. He was with us. That's made him more stronger than we had two trumpets, you see?
You think it was the swing then, the special good swing you had that made you popular.
That's right.
When you played for dances, did you play mostly jazz numbers or waltz numbers sometimes?

Or what kind of pieces did you play? We played everything. We played waltzes. We had some places we played, we had to play shorters. And Frenchman downtown you had to play a shorters like at E climbing hall you had to play a shorters. Once in about 11 o'clock or 12 o'clock. I don't know if you ever seen one of them dance.
No, I think maybe I saw slow drag demonstrated once, you know, slow drag, Pauvajon the bass player. But I don't know anything about it.

Well, they had, they used to dance them for prizes. Now these little youngsters, they have to sit on. They had to sit on. The guys used to sit on a glass of water right up on their head and they danced. And don't waste a drap. They just turned around and all the way around, right and left. Then we played waltzes, like two waltzes. We played two blues. We played mostly jazz numbers. Well, we played the blues around about 12 o'clock. Well, we looked for a fight then, you understand. Why do the blues do that?
I never could figure that out. I'm not sure.

Well, I don't understand. And the way they're playing blues now, they just, I don't know, the way they're playing the blues now, they're jumping them. And it just seems like it makes the people feel frigid or good. You understand what I mean? But the blues that we used to play, like them slow drag blues, you hear the people screaming when we start to play. Well then the guys will start to fight. I guess that might work on the nerves or something. I don't know. What about the women?
It must have affected them too, huh?
It must have affected them. More so. More than the men.
Did you have many vocalists in those days in the band? Did anybody do any singing? No, no, no, no.

Just maybe some fella out the audience would come up there and try to sing. Guys wasn't thinking about singing then. They are, the most of the people with singing would be people in the dance hall. And they don't think about singing. We wouldn't have, we didn't have no vocal, but now you've got to have somebody sing something. If you ever do like Louis Armstrong, just jive your way through.
What about brass bands? What was the first brass band you ever played with?

Who me? I haven't played, well, yes, I played two parades in New Orleans since I've been a musician. I played on Labor Day. I played with Sam and Chris Kelly. They was playing a brass band. Playing a parade. And they fooled me. And I didn't want to go and play. And they asked me to play. And I played from Louisiana Avenue down to Connell Street. And them cats was laying down on them, you know. And they want to open up when they got over Connell Street, you see. And when they did get over Connell Street, Kelly could blow and Sam could blow. And then man, my lips would swore up like that. They just had them blowed me to death, you see. And they made me play the whole lot. That's the time that Ruth Gordon was running down there, the temple Ruth Gordon. So I said I wouldn't play in no more parade. So somebody, they begged me and begged me. Edgar, he's in Chicago now. They were short of a man that played a fume. And it was over in Algae. And he said they were just going to play some church hymns. And when I played a fume, I said, well, I don't like to play no fume. And the big men, big men, I went and played that fume with them. That's the only two parades I ever played. I don't, I just don't like to walk and play.
What did Ed Gunn play, one instrument? The drum. Is that Bat's brother? Yeah. Ed Gunn Moses. Yeah.
That was one of Howard boys.
Yeah. Did you ever run across Chris Kelly much over there along the coast in Biloxi or Mobile or any place?
Chris Kelly's dead.
Yeah, no, but I mean in the old days, did he ever come over there when you were playing much? No, no, no, no.
He didn't, he didn't used to come over there. The fellas used to, was in that, was in power, them was old Foster, Foster, Foster, Foster and his brother.
Dude. Huh? That dude's brother?

Dude. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, them was, when they used to come over, they used to go over there. Well Sam used to keep the course hot before I ever got the first chance to go over there. And how come they go over there, a handy saxophone player, I guess you know him, eh? Oh yeah.
He's my janitor.

Well, his daddy was playing bass violin and old Tom Albin on Begundry and St. Peter. Tom used to be his trumpet player. And they always wanted to carry me over there. And they carried me to Passpegoula. That's the first time I had a chance to get over there. And after I got over there once, then this, the fellow was running the pressing shop. He seen me. And Tom and them couldn't come and asked me could I get a band. I told him yeah. And we was, I said, young Sam Morgan band. And we went over there and from that on, we just kept a going on there.
I wondered in 1915 when you moved up here, who the best trumpet players were in the carnet, on the carnet in this city. Do you remember Oliver or Kepard or anybody like that?

I remember Juaro, Manuel Perez. I used to like to hear them men play trumpet because it takes three trumpet players to play them fumes and parades. And them too used to play the parade, you see. And both of them was loud and they could play. You see them. Joe Oliver and Manuel Perez. Now Freddie Carford, I heard him a couple of times but I don't know, he just got on out of my sight. I didn't, I never was around no place where he was playing regular. He went on away.
Did you hear Bunk Johnson? Was he here in those days?

Well, nah. Bunk, he was, he was, he was here a while and then he moved on up to, up to country somewhere. But he wasn't playing, he knew me but I didn't know him. He was playing, he was playing dances around there but I didn't know, I didn't know him. When he come here with George Lewis, he knew me right at the corner where I stood. But I didn't know him.
He seemed to know everybody. Were there any other good trumpet players you can remember when you first moved up here, some of the oldest ones that were popular or that you thought were good?
Well outside of Manny Perez, and Joe Oliver, and Louis Armstrong, them about the only three men that I knew.
Which was the most popular band? Do you remember the most popular bands then? What the?
For dance bands?
Well, Joe Oliver.

It becomes Fess. Joe Oliver had a, a, a tough band. Was Ori playing much then? Well yeah, I, I was, I used to, I used to hire men. I used to play them picnics up there with us until he, until he, until he moved. We're just about two here.
No, trust me. Okay, we're just about two here in 10 seconds. Well, it'll be about five. Oh yeah, I'll be, I'll be here.
Alright, see you later. Alright, see you later.

Ori had a good band and Jack Carey. Oh yes. Well them was famous bands, Jack Carey, and that's the time we was advertising then. On trucks for, for, for, for dancers, you see. Did your band play on those trucks at the L2, to advertise? Oh man, sure. T.L. gate, man, you hang, back up, like that call backing up there and tie up there in the stadium and play yourself crazy. What they was doing that for, I don't know. Man, every time they see a band, they'll catch them. Make them play. Stop them and buck them. To see who could play, who, play the longest. I grabbed a little punch one day.
